origin: Greek isos, equal, and tropos, a turn or direction.

meanings.short: The same in every direction.
meanings.long: Something is isotropic when no direction is special: measured along any direction it gives the same result. A gas in a box has isotropic pressure; the universe, averaged over large scales, looks isotropic from Earth.

origin: Greek homos, same, and genos, kind.

meanings.short: The same at every place.
meanings.long: Something is homogeneous when every place in it is like every other: the same density, the same temperature, the same laws. It does not say every direction looks the same; that is isotropic.

meanings.short: Of a linear equation: with zero on the right-hand side, so that zero is a solution; its solutions form the homogeneous solution.
meanings.long: The equation y'' + y = 0 is homogeneous; y'' + y = cos t is not, because of the cos t on the right. The general solution of the second is any one particular solution plus every solution of the first.

meanings.short: Of a linear equation: with zero on the right-hand side, so that zero is a solution.
meanings.long: A homogeneous equation has no term free of the unknown; adding a driving term or a source makes it inhomogeneous.

meanings.short: Of a function: unchanged in form when every variable is multiplied by the same number, apart from a power of that number.
meanings.long: A function f is homogeneous of degree k when f(λx, λy) equals λ to the power k times f(x, y). Such functions turn up in substitutions for differential equations and in symmetry arguments.

meanings.short: Of a linear equation: with a term free of the unknown on the right-hand side, so the sum of two solutions is no longer one.
meanings.long: Adding a constant force or a source term to a linear equation makes it inhomogeneous. Without that term the equation is homogeneous and any sum of solutions is again a solution.

meanings.short: Known or assumed before looking at any evidence.
meanings.long: An a priori argument starts from principles or assumptions rather than from measurements. The opposite is a posteriori, known from experience.

meanings.short: A shortened form of a word or phrase, such as "eq." for equation.

everyday: Not "vague": abstract mathematics is exact, only not tied to one concrete example.

meanings.short: Thought of in general terms, apart from any particular object or picture.
meanings.long: An abstract vector space has the rules of arrows without needing any arrows. The extra generality lets one result serve many cases.

meanings.short: Writing that bends the strict rules of the symbols for convenience, when the meaning is still clear.
Explains, makes up a stated share of, or takes into account something.
meanings.long: "Dark energy accounts for about 70% of the total" means it makes up that share; "the model accounts for the data" means it explains them; "a derivative has to account for that" means it must allow for it.

meanings.short: Closeness to the true value: an accurate measurement or calculation gives a result near the right answer.
meanings.long: Accuracy differs from precision: a precise measurement gives nearly the same value each time, but an accurate one gives the right value.

meanings.short: Made up for one particular case, with no deeper reason behind it.
meanings.long: An ad hoc assumption or fix is added just to make one result come out right, rather than following from a general principle. Physicists treat ad hoc fixes with suspicion, because they explain nothing beyond the case they were made for.

origin: Greek aisthetikos, to do with the senses.

meanings.short: To do with beauty or taste, rather than with evidence.
Open to more than one meaning, so it is unclear which is intended.
Something that behaves like something else in an important way.
meanings.long: An electric circuit with a coil and capacitor is an analogue of a mass on a spring: the same equation describes both.

meanings.short: A comparison that explains one thing by pointing to a similar, better-known one.
meanings.long: Analogies help understanding but can mislead where the two things differ: the expanding balloon is a famous example.

meanings.short: Something that does not fit the expected pattern or the accepted theory.
meanings.long: The anomalous advance of Mercury's orbit could not be explained by Newton's gravity; general relativity accounted for it.

origin: German, a starting point or set-up.

meanings.short: A guessed form for a solution, with some numbers left open, to be fixed by putting the guess into the equation.
meanings.long: Physicists often write down an ansatz such as "try y = e to the power rt" and then find which values of r make it work. If the guess leads to a consistent answer, it was a good ansatz; if not, a different form is tried.

meanings.short: Large enough to notice or to matter.
Close to, but not exactly, the true value; an approximation is such a value or formula, chosen because it is simpler.
meanings.long: Physics uses approximations everywhere: small angles, low speeds, weak fields. A good approximation states its error, or at least when it stops being reliable.

everyday: Not "unfair" or "without reason": it means "any one you like".

meanings.short: Free to be chosen as one likes; any choice gives a correct result.
meanings.long: "An arbitrary constant" can take any value; "arbitrarily small" means as small as you wish. The word does not mean random or unfair.

meanings.short: Understood by very few; obscure and specialised.
As one could reasonably claim, though not everyone would agree.

everyday: Not a quarrel: an argument is a line of reasoning.

meanings.short: A chain of reasoning that leads to a conclusion; in maths also the input of a function, such as x in sin x.
meanings.long: In science writing, "the argument" is the reasoning, not a quarrel. In mathematics the argument of a function is what it acts on, and the argument of a complex number is its angle.

meanings.short: A free website where physicists and mathematicians post research papers, often before a journal publishes them.
Something accepted as true, without proof, so that an argument or calculation can proceed; to assume is to accept it so.
meanings.long: Every model rests on assumptions, such as that the universe is the same everywhere. A result is only as reliable as the assumptions behind it.

meanings.short: As it first appears, without questioning or checking it further.
Helping or extra: introduced to help with a calculation, not of interest in itself.
meanings.long: An auxiliary variable or state is brought in to make a problem easier to solve, and may drop out of the final answer.

meanings.short: Cancels over many values or a long time, because positive and negative parts balance.
meanings.long: Random errors average out over many measurements; fast wiggles average out over a long time.

origin: Greek axioma, what is thought worthy.

meanings.short: A basic rule accepted without proof, from which a branch of mathematics is built.
meanings.long: Euclid's geometry starts from a handful of axioms, one of them the parallel postulate; changing that one gives the curved geometries of cosmology. In linear algebra, the rules a vector space must obey are also called axioms.

meanings.short: A standard example or value used to test or compare others.

everyday: Not "explode": in maths it means "become infinite".

meanings.short: In maths, to grow without limit; to become infinite.
meanings.long: "The solution blows up at t = 1" means it becomes infinitely large as t approaches 1.

meanings.short: To enlarge a picture of a small region so its detail can be seen.

everyday: Not accounting for money: in physics it means keeping careful track of terms.

meanings.short: In calculations, careful tracking of terms, signs, indices or factors so that none is lost.
meanings.long: Much of the work in long derivations is bookkeeping: the ideas are simple, but every factor must be accounted for.

meanings.short: On the boundary between two kinds of behaviour, belonging clearly to neither.
meanings.long: In a stability analysis the borderline cases, exactly between stable and unstable, often need extra care.

meanings.short: Solving a problem by direct, laborious calculation rather than by a clever shortcut.
Multiplied or divided by the stated number.
meanings.long: "The density fell by a factor of 8" means it became one eighth as large; "grew by a factor of 2" means it doubled.

meanings.short: True because it was taken as given at the start of the argument, not because it was shown.
True because of the way the thing was built or chosen, so no separate check is needed.
meanings.long: If a function is made by adding a term chosen to cancel a problem, the problem is gone by construction.

meanings.short: True simply because of what the words or symbols were set up to mean, not because of any further fact.
meanings.long: A statement true by definition needs no measurement or proof: it only restates the definition.

meanings.short: Judged just by looking, without measuring or calculating.
Worked out with pen and paper, without a computer; or put in deliberately rather than following from the theory.
meanings.long: A constant "put in by hand" is chosen to fit, not predicted. A sum done "by hand" is done without a computer.

meanings.short: To set or correct a measuring method by comparing it with a known standard.
meanings.long: Astronomers calibrate the brightness of distant supernovae using nearby ones whose distances are known by other means.

meanings.short: Still applies, with little change, in a new setting.
meanings.long: "The argument carries over to three dimensions" means the same reasoning works there too.

everyday: Not a funny drawing: a scientific cartoon is a simplified sketch.

meanings.short: In science talk, a deliberately simplified picture of a process, showing the idea rather than exact details.
A warning or condition that limits a statement.
meanings.long: "With one caveat" means the claim holds, but with an exception or a condition to keep in mind.

meanings.short: A note saying exactly where a statement, number or formula comes from, so readers can check it.
meanings.long: This site cites every formula to a place in the MIT material, such as a slide number or a transcript page.

meanings.short: Sharply defined and easy to decide, with no doubtful cases.
A striking agreement between two things that seems to happen by chance, with no known reason.
meanings.long: Physicists distrust coincidences: an unexplained agreement between two numbers often hints at a hidden connection.

meanings.short: Is, in the end, simply a matter of.
Of roughly the same size, so neither can be ignored next to the other.
meanings.long: "The wavelength is comparable to the slit width" means the two are about equal, which is when diffraction matters most.

meanings.short: Strongly convincing, so that it is hard not to accept.
Possible to imagine or think of, though perhaps unlikely.
To do with ideas and understanding rather than calculation.
Settling a question beyond reasonable doubt.
A statement believed to be true but not yet proved.
meanings.long: In mathematics a conjecture stays open until someone proves or disproves it. In physics the word is also used for an educated guess about how nature works.

meanings.short: Agreeing with, and not contradicting, something else, such as the data, another result, or itself.
meanings.long: "The result is consistent with the measurement" means the two agree within the uncertainties. A consistent theory never leads to two answers that contradict each other.

meanings.short: Of separate effects, to combine as if by plan to produce a result.
Arranged artificially to get a wanted result, rather than arising naturally.
Causing strong disagreement among experts.
An agreed choice, such as which direction counts as positive, that could have been made differently.
meanings.long: Sign conventions and unit conventions differ between books; results agree once the same conventions are used. "Conventional" can also mean "usual".

meanings.short: Usual and standard, following the accepted way; or fixed by an agreed choice.
meanings.long: "The conventional Big Bang" means the standard version of the theory, before inflation was added. "Conventionally positive" means positive by agreement.

meanings.short: The statement made by swapping the 'if' and 'then' parts of another statement.
meanings.long: The converse of "if A then B" is "if B then A". It need not be true when the original is: every square is a rectangle, but not every rectangle is a square.

meanings.short: Turning the statement round: what follows is the same idea seen from the other side.
meanings.long: "Conversely" introduces the reverse of a previous statement, which may or may not also be true and is stated separately.

origin: Latin corollarium, a gift or extra.

meanings.short: A result that follows directly from one just proved, with little or no extra work.
Going against what one would naturally expect, though true.
meanings.long: Many results of relativity and quantum mechanics are counter-intuitive because everyday experience never shows them.

meanings.short: A single case showing that a general claim is false.
meanings.long: One counterexample is enough to disprove a statement that claims to hold always.

meanings.short: Something that plays the same role in another setting.
meanings.long: "The classical counterpart of a quantum number" means the quantity that does the same job in classical physics.

origin: Greek kriterion, a means of judging.

meanings.short: A test or rule used to decide something, such as whether a system is stable.
meanings.long: Named criteria, like the Jeans criterion for collapse, state a condition: if it holds, one outcome follows. The plural is criteria.

meanings.short: Rough and simple, accurate only to the general size of the answer.
A long-running disagreement among experts, argued out with evidence and reasoning.
In a way that gives a false impression; deceptively simple means harder than it looks.
To reach a conclusion by reasoning from what is already known.
Needing great care, because a small mistake or a small change can spoil the result.
meanings.long: "A delicate cancellation" means two large numbers almost cancel, so tiny errors in either matter a lot.

meanings.short: To stand for; to be the symbol or name used for something.
meanings.long: "Let v denote the velocity" means the letter v will be used for the velocity.

meanings.short: To obtain a result by reasoning or calculation from other known results.
meanings.long: A derivation is the chain of steps from starting assumptions to a result. Deriving a formula, rather than just quoting it, shows where it comes from and when it holds.

meanings.short: Decreases gradually towards zero and then no longer matters.
meanings.long: A damped oscillation dies out: its size shrinks with time until nothing is left.

meanings.short: A difference between two things that should agree, such as a prediction and a measurement.
To be the largest contribution, so that the others hardly matter.
meanings.long: "Radiation dominates the early universe" means radiation's energy density far exceeds that of matter then, so it sets how the universe expands.

meanings.short: Disappears from an equation, usually because it cancels or appears on both sides.
meanings.long: "The mass drops out" means it cancels, so the answer does not depend on it.

origin: Latin exempli gratia, for the sake of example.

meanings.short: For example: introduces one or more examples, not a complete list.
meanings.long: Written before examples: "heavy elements, e.g. carbon and oxygen". Do not confuse it with i.e., which introduces a restatement.

meanings.short: A guess guided by knowledge and experience, likely to be close.

everyday: In everyday English it often means "successfully"; in science it usually means "as good as" or "in effect".

meanings.short: For all practical purposes; behaving as if it were so, even though strictly it is not.
meanings.long: "Neutrinos are effectively massless at high temperature" means their small mass makes no noticeable difference there. Usually the word does not mean "efficiently".

meanings.short: Simple, short and clear in a way that seems to reveal how things really fit together.
meanings.long: An elegant proof or theory uses few assumptions and little calculation. Elegance is not evidence, but physicists often take it as a good sign.

meanings.short: An obvious, important problem that everyone avoids mentioning.
Arising from the combined behaviour of many parts, though no single part has it.
meanings.long: Temperature is emergent: one molecule has none, but a gas of many does.

meanings.short: Based on observation or measurement rather than derived from theory.
meanings.long: An empirical law, such as a fitted relation between brightness and period, describes data well before anyone can explain it.

meanings.short: Equation: followed by its number in the source, as in Eq. 3.12; Eqs. means equations.

everyday: Not necessarily a mistake: in science an error is the expected difference from the true value.

meanings.short: The difference between a measured or computed value and the true one; often how large that difference may be.
meanings.long: In science, "error" usually means uncertainty, not a mistake: every measurement has some. An approximation's error is how far it is from the exact answer.

meanings.short: And others: written after the first author's name when a paper has several authors.
meanings.long: "Riess et al. (1998)" means a paper by Riess and co-authors. Science papers often have many authors, so only the first is named.

origin: Latin et cetera, and the rest.

meanings.short: And so on: more things of the same kind follow but are not listed.
Covering every possible case, with nothing left out.
Unusual and unlike ordinary, familiar matter or behaviour.
meanings.long: "Exotic matter" might have negative energy density; "exotic particles" are ones not yet observed. The word says the thing is unfamiliar, not that it is foreign.

meanings.short: Stated or written out directly and in full, with nothing left to be worked out.
meanings.long: An explicit formula gives the answer directly, such as y = x squared, rather than as an equation still to be solved.

meanings.short: To extend a trend beyond the range where it was measured, assuming it continues.
meanings.long: Running the expansion of the universe backwards to find its age is an extrapolation; it is only as good as the assumption that the same laws held.

meanings.short: Coming from outside, or depending on how a thing sits within something larger.
meanings.long: Extrinsic curvature describes how a surface bends within the space around it, as opposed to curvature measured within the surface itself.

meanings.short: Decreases as something grows, usually with distance.
meanings.long: "The field falls off as one over r squared" means it gets smaller in proportion to one over the distance squared.

meanings.short: To show by evidence that a theory or claim is false.
meanings.long: A scientific theory must be falsifiable: some possible observation would prove it wrong.

meanings.short: Very unlikely and hard to believe.
Chosen as a standard reference value or model, against which others are compared.
Figure: a numbered picture or diagram in the source; Figs. means figures.
The most basic laws or assumptions, from which a result is derived without borrowing other results.
The basis or standing of something; things on an equal footing are treated in exactly the same way.
meanings.long: "Coordinates and momenta on an equal footing" means neither is treated as more basic than the other: both are independent variables of the same rank.

meanings.short: In every way that matters for the job at hand, though not exactly or strictly.
A particular mathematical way of writing and working with a theory.
meanings.long: The same physics can be described in different formalisms, for example Newton's forces or Lagrange's energies. Choosing a good one can make a hard problem easy.

meanings.short: Following the rules or symbols exactly as written, sometimes without checking that each step makes sense.
meanings.long: "Divide formally by dx" means treat dx as if it were an ordinary number, which gives the right answer though it needs justifying. "Formally infinite" means infinite if the formula is taken literally.

meanings.short: The basic structure of ideas and equations inside which more detailed theories or calculations are set up.
meanings.long: General relativity is a framework: many different models of the universe can be built inside it.

meanings.short: Leading to many useful results.
A number put into a formula to make it agree with the answer wanted, without a full justification.
meanings.long: Sometimes a fudge factor is later explained by a deeper theory; until then it is a sign that something is missing.

meanings.short: The quality of applying to many cases, not only to one particular example.
meanings.long: "In full generality" means for every case the statement covers, with no simplifying assumptions.

meanings.short: Typical of most cases, with no special feature or coincidence.
meanings.long: A generic point on a curve is not a peak or a crossing; a generic matrix has all its eigenvalues different. Special cases are the exceptions to the generic one.

meanings.short: Said too easily and quickly, without enough thought or care.
Loose, informal reasoning that makes a claim sound plausible without really showing it.
meanings.long: Used of an argument that skips the hard steps. It is not always bad: it can give the right idea quickly, as long as the reader knows the careful version is missing.

meanings.short: Speaking cautiously so as not to commit firmly to a claim.
For this reason; as a result of what was just said.
meanings.long: "The mass is constant, hence the momentum changes only through the velocity." In older writing it can also mean "from here" or "from now".

meanings.short: Rough but useful reasoning that gives a likely answer or insight without being a full proof.
meanings.long: A heuristic argument explains why a result should be true, often with a simple picture, while leaving out the careful steps a proof would need.

meanings.short: Understanding of a situation that comes only after it has happened.
A proposed explanation that can be tested by observation or experiment.
meanings.long: A hypothesis is a starting point for investigation, not yet a settled result. In a mathematical statement, the hypotheses are the conditions that must hold for the conclusion to follow.

meanings.short: In mathematics, a condition a theorem assumes; or a statement not yet proved, such as the Riemann hypothesis.
meanings.long: "The theorem has two hypotheses" means it holds only when both conditions are met.

meanings.short: Imagined or supposed for the sake of argument, not known to exist.
meanings.long: A hypothetical particle is one a theory proposes but no experiment has yet detected.

meanings.short: That is: introduces a clearer or more exact way of saying what was just said.
meanings.long: Written before a restatement: "the scale factor is constant, i.e. nothing expands". Do not confuse it with e.g., which introduces examples.

meanings.short: Simplified to a perfect case that does not quite exist, such as a frictionless slope or a point mass.
meanings.long: Idealisations remove effects that are small or beside the point, so the main physics can be calculated. A real system differs from its idealisation by small corrections.

meanings.short: In exactly the same way; in maths, for every value of the variable, as when a function is zero everywhere.
meanings.long: "Identically distributed" variables all follow the same probability law. A function that vanishes identically is the zero function, not one that is zero only at some points.

meanings.short: Without a clear single meaning or value, for example because different methods give different answers.
Helping to make an idea clear and easy to understand.
Contained in or following from something without being written out directly.
meanings.long: An implicit assumption is made without being stated. A function given implicitly is defined by an equation it satisfies, rather than by a formula for it.

meanings.short: A lasting mark or pattern left on something by an earlier event.
meanings.long: Sound waves in the early universe left their imprint on the cosmic microwave background as a pattern of hot and cold spots.

meanings.short: In a few words; summed up as briefly as possible.
Partly, or when looked at in one particular way; not in every respect.
Looking different on the surface but really the same as something already known.
meanings.long: "Pythagoras in disguise" means a formula that, once rewritten, turns out to be Pythagoras' theorem. Spotting such disguises is a common way to simplify a problem.

meanings.short: In practice, as far as the result goes, even if not literally or officially so.
Briefly, while dealing with something else, without stopping to discuss it fully.
In reality, as things are actually done or measured, rather than in theory.
According to the rules or theory, even if it would be hard or impossible to do in reality.
meanings.long: "In principle we could compute the motion of every molecule" means nothing in the laws forbids it, though in practice it is far too much work.

meanings.short: Following the same basic idea or approach as something else, without copying it exactly.
One after another, in order; or as the next link in a chain of causes.
meanings.long: "Each mode appears in turn" means one after the other. "A heats B, which in turn heats C" means B then passes the effect on to C.

meanings.short: To conclude something from evidence, rather than see it directly.
meanings.long: The amount of dark matter is inferred from how fast stars orbit, not seen directly.

meanings.short: One of the parts or assumptions that go into a theory, model or calculation.
meanings.long: "The key ingredient is gravity" means gravity is the essential element without which the result would not follow.

meanings.short: A clear, deep understanding of how or why something works.
Useful to study because it teaches something.
To estimate a value between two known values.
Belonging to the thing itself, not depending on how it is viewed or where it is placed.
meanings.long: The intrinsic brightness of a star is how much light it gives out, not how bright it looks from here. Intrinsic curvature can be measured from inside a space without looking at it from outside.

meanings.short: A feeling for what should be true, built from experience, before working it out.
Easy to understand or believe at once, without detailed reasoning.
To repeat a step again and again, each time starting from the previous result.
meanings.long: An iterative method improves a guess by repeating the same rule; each repeat is one iteration. In the study of maps, the iterates are the successive values produced.

everyday: Informal maths language for "turns into zero".

meanings.short: In maths slang, to make a term or vector zero.
meanings.long: "Setting x = 0 kills every term with an x in it" means those terms become zero. A matrix kills the vectors it sends to zero.

meanings.short: Needing a lot of work and time.
The second of two things just mentioned.
meanings.long: "The former" is the first of two things mentioned, "the latter" the second.

meanings.short: The first and largest part of an answer, keeping only the main term and dropping smaller corrections.
meanings.long: A calculation "to leading order" keeps the term that dominates; corrections come at the next order and are smaller.

meanings.short: Allowed by the rules; correct and justified.
A smaller result proved first, as a stepping stone towards a more important theorem.
Stops rising or falling and settles at a steady value.
In the same way; similarly.
A situation at the extreme of a range, where some quantity is very large or very small.
meanings.long: Checking limiting cases, such as zero mass or infinite distance, is a quick test that a formula makes sense.

everyday: In everyday English "literature" means novels, poems and plays; in science it means published research.

meanings.short: The body of published research papers and books on a subject.
meanings.long: "Estimates in the literature range from 3 to 5 minutes" means published scientific work gives that range.

everyday: Not engines or machines: here it means a well-developed set of mathematical tools.

meanings.short: In maths and physics, the set of methods and formulas used to carry out a type of calculation.
meanings.long: "The machinery of curvature" means the formulas that turn a metric into curvature; once set up, it can be applied without rethinking each step.

meanings.short: Plainly, so that it can be seen at a glance from the way it is written.
meanings.long: A formula is manifestly symmetric when its symmetry is obvious from its form, without any calculation.

everyday: Informal: "massaging" an equation means reshaping it, not changing what it says.

meanings.short: In maths slang, to rearrange an expression step by step into a more useful form.
The process or chain of causes by which something happens; also a device of moving parts.
meanings.long: Asking for the mechanism of an effect means asking how it comes about, step by step, not only that it happens.

meanings.short: In calculations, long and complicated, with many terms, though not hard in principle.
An exam held in the middle of a university term, covering the first part of a course.

everyday: Not supernatural: physicists use it for a happy surprise in a calculation.

meanings.short: In physics talk, a surprising and lucky result that makes something work out with no obvious reason.
Of a function or formula, to fail to be smooth or finite somewhere, so that the usual rules break.
A mistake in printed text, such as a wrong sign or number.
Massachusetts Institute of Technology: the university in Cambridge, USA, whose free courses this site rewrites.
meanings.long: MIT publishes the notes, slides, videos and problem sets of many of its courses on OpenCourseWare. Most lessons here follow an MIT lecture, in MIT's order; one Year V course follows an open textbook instead.

everyday: Not a small copy of something: a model in science is usually a set of equations.

meanings.short: A simplified description of a real system, usually in equations, that keeps what matters and leaves out the rest.
meanings.long: A model of the universe may treat galaxies as a smooth fluid; a model of a gas may treat molecules as tiny hard balls. A good model is simple enough to solve and accurate enough to compare with measurement.

everyday: Not about right and wrong: "the moral" here is the lesson.

meanings.short: The general lesson to take away from an example or argument.
In addition; and also, adding a further point to the argument.

everyday: Not "encourage a person": here it means "give a reason for".

meanings.short: In science writing, to give a reason for introducing or trying something.
meanings.long: "This motivates the definition" means it explains why the definition is a natural one to make.

everyday: Not "foolish": in science it means "the simplest first attempt".

meanings.short: Simple and first-guess, without the corrections or care a fuller treatment adds.
meanings.long: "A naive estimate" is the first answer one gets by the obvious route; it is often wrong in an instructive way. The word is not an insult here.

meanings.short: That is to say: introduces the exact thing that was just described in general terms.

everyday: Not "forget" or "fail to look after": in science it is a deliberate choice.

meanings.short: To leave out on purpose, because the effect is too small to matter.
So small that leaving it out makes no noticeable difference to the result.
meanings.long: A term is negligible when its effect is far below the accuracy needed, for example air resistance on a dropped stone over one metre.

meanings.short: Not a matter of chance: there is a deeper reason why it happens.
Not obvious: needing real work or thought; in maths, a solution other than the obvious zero one.
A system of symbols used to write ideas down briefly, such as dy/dx for a derivative.
meanings.long: Different notations for the same idea, like Newton's dots and Leibniz's d's, can make a calculation easier or harder.

meanings.short: An idea or concept, often one not yet made fully precise.
In terms of actual numbers rather than symbols; often worked out step by step, by computer, instead of from an exact formula.
meanings.long: A numerical solution of a differential equation follows the answer in small steps; it is approximate but works when no formula exists.

meanings.short: A reason given against an idea or an argument.
OpenCourseWare: MIT's free website of course materials, the source of every MIT lesson on this site.
meanings.long: OCW publishes lecture notes, slides, transcripts, videos and problem sets under an open licence that allows them to be reused and adapted, as this site does.

meanings.short: Roughly equal to, within a factor of a few; of order one means neither much bigger nor much smaller than one.
meanings.long: "Of order 10 to the power 5" means somewhere near a hundred thousand. Physicists drop factors of order one in rough estimates.

meanings.short: In theory or in a calculation, as opposed to in a real experiment or in reality.
Exactly; precisely right, with no error at all.
The start of something, especially a change of behaviour.
A question nobody has yet answered.
A factor of about ten; an order-of-magnitude estimate gets only the power of ten right.
meanings.long: Two numbers differ by three orders of magnitude when one is about 1000 times the other. Order-of-magnitude reasoning checks whether an effect is large or tiny before doing exact work.

meanings.short: Page, in a reference to a source; pp. means pages, as in pp. 3–5.
meanings.long: Citations on this site say where in the MIT material something comes from, for example "transcript p. 4" for page 4 of the lecture transcript.

meanings.short: A widely accepted way of thinking about a subject, which shapes what questions people ask.
meanings.long: Cold dark matter is the current paradigm for how galaxies form: most work assumes it, though it is still tested.

origin: Greek para, against, and doxa, opinion.

meanings.short: A statement or situation that seems to contradict itself, though it may turn out not to.
meanings.long: The twin paradox seems to break the symmetry of relativity; it is resolved by noticing that one twin accelerates. Most paradoxes in physics point to a hidden assumption.

everyday: Not about illness: in maths and physics it means "badly behaved".

meanings.short: Behaving in a strange, extreme or badly behaved way, so that the usual rules fail; of an example built to break a rule.
meanings.long: A pathological function has, for instance, infinitely many wiggles or no derivative anywhere. Physicists often set such cases aside as unphysical.

meanings.short: The useful result that makes earlier effort worthwhile.
A person who insists on small details of exactness, often more than the situation needs.
Describing what is observed with a formula that fits, without deriving it from deeper theory.
meanings.long: A phenomenological model captures the data with a few adjustable numbers; a fundamental model explains where those numbers come from.

meanings.short: Something that happens and can be observed, such as an eclipse or a rainbow.
meanings.long: The plural is phenomena.

meanings.short: To fix exactly, leaving no freedom or doubt.
meanings.long: "Two conditions pin down the two constants" means they determine both constants completely.

meanings.short: A hidden or easily made mistake.
A symbol or word that temporarily stands in for something to be filled in later.
Reasonable and likely to be true, though not proved.
To put numbers or expressions into a formula in place of its symbols.
A basic statement taken as true without proof, as a starting point from which other results are derived.
meanings.long: Special relativity rests on two postulates: the laws of physics are the same for all inertial observers, and light has the same speed for all of them. As a verb, to postulate is to assume something exists or is true in order to build a theory.

meanings.short: How finely a measurement is made, or how close repeated measurements are to each other.
meanings.long: A precise result has small scatter; it can still be inaccurate if every measurement is off in the same way.

meanings.short: Coming before the main part; early and not yet final.
A research paper shared publicly before it has been checked and printed by a journal.
meanings.long: Physicists post preprints, mostly on the arXiv website, so new results spread at once instead of months later.

meanings.short: Something you need to know or have done before you can start something else.
meanings.long: Each lesson lists its prerequisites: earlier lessons whose ideas it builds on.

meanings.short: Very likely, as one would reasonably suppose, though nobody has checked it.
meanings.long: On this site it often marks a guess about what a lecturer meant, for example where a slide seems to contain a slip.

meanings.short: Specially favoured or singled out over the others.
meanings.long: "There is no privileged coordinate system" means no choice of coordinates is more correct than another.

meanings.short: A weekly sheet of exercises that students work through and hand in, to practise what the lectures taught.
meanings.long: MIT courses set one problem set most weeks; this site has its own problem sets with hints and worked solutions.

meanings.short: A person who supports and argues for an idea.
Accepted for now, but expected to change when more is known.
The key result or conclusion that a long argument leads up to.
About the kind or shape of behaviour, not its exact numbers.
meanings.long: A qualitative picture says that a ball slows and turns back; a quantitative one says when and where.

meanings.short: To measure or express as a number.
In numbers; giving exact amounts rather than only the general behaviour.
To take a value directly from a graph, table or formula, without further calculation.
A reply that argues against a claim, trying to show it is wrong.
A short summary of what has already been covered.

origin: Latin, take! (the first word of old prescriptions).

meanings.short: A fixed series of steps that, followed in order, always gives the answer.
meanings.long: Many standard problems have a recipe: write the energy, take the derivatives, solve. Knowing why each step works is what turns a recipe into understanding.

meanings.short: At MIT, a small class led by a teacher or assistant, where students go over problems and questions from the main lectures.
meanings.long: Recitations go with the large lectures of a course. Some MIT courses publish their recitation notes too.

meanings.short: Not needed, because the same information is already given elsewhere.
meanings.long: A redundant equation follows from the others and adds nothing new.

meanings.short: To prove a claim or theory wrong.

everyday: Not a government: in science a regime is a range of conditions.

meanings.short: A range of conditions in which one kind of behaviour holds, such as a particular range of speeds or temperatures.
meanings.long: "In the radiation-dominated regime" means during the period, or under the conditions, when radiation sets the behaviour. Outside its regime, a simple formula may fail.

meanings.short: Bringing to mind something similar.
In the order given: the first item goes with the first, the second with the second, and so on.
meanings.long: "The masses of A and B are 2 kg and 3 kg, respectively" means A has 2 kg and B has 3 kg.

meanings.short: A public withdrawal of a claim or paper that its author now thinks is wrong.
meanings.long: Einstein published a retraction of his objection to Friedmann's expanding solutions once he saw his own mistake.

meanings.short: Careful and exact in every step, so that nothing is assumed without proof.
meanings.long: A rigorous derivation leaves no gaps; physicists often give a quicker, less rigorous argument and trust that the careful version exists.

meanings.short: Holding firm when the details or assumptions are changed a little.
meanings.long: A robust prediction does not depend on one uncertain number; it survives many variations of the model.

meanings.short: A quick, approximate value, worked out without care for small details.
A simple practical rule, roughly right in most cases, used instead of an exact calculation.
To show that a possibility cannot be right, so it is no longer considered.
meanings.long: "The data rule out a closed universe of that size" means the measurements are inconsistent with it.

meanings.short: A quick test that an answer is sensible, such as checking its units or its size.
meanings.long: Typical sanity checks: does the answer have the right units, the right sign, and the right behaviour in a simple limiting case?

everyday: Not "please": in maths it means "fulfil" or "obey".

meanings.short: To make an equation or condition true.
meanings.long: "x = 2 satisfies x squared = 4" means putting 2 in makes the equation true. A function satisfies a differential equation when it solves it.

meanings.short: One possible sequence of events, or one version of a theory, considered to see what it predicts.
A person who doubts a claim until convincing evidence is shown.
Showing only the main features in a simplified way, not to scale or exactly.
Agreeing with its own assumptions; in a calculation, an answer that, fed back in as an assumption, gives itself again.
meanings.long: In a self-consistent treatment each particle feels an average field made by all the others, and that field is adjusted until it reproduces itself.

meanings.short: Clearly true without needing any proof or explanation.
A short way of writing something longer, such as a symbol standing for a whole expression.
Large enough to matter or to be noticed; in statistics, too large to put down to chance.
meanings.long: A significant correction changes the answer noticeably. A statistically significant result is unlikely to come from random scatter; such an effect can still be small.

meanings.short: In 'significant figures': the digits of a number that carry real information about its value.
meanings.long: A value written 3.14 has three significant figures; more digits would claim a precision the value does not have.

meanings.short: Picks out one thing as special among many.
In science talk, a method far more powerful and laborious than the problem needs.
Details and conditions that are easy to miss but matter.
A piece of evidence that settles a question beyond doubt.
One particular example of a general rule, obtained by fixing some of its quantities.
meanings.long: Hooke's law is a special case of the general behaviour of a force near a stable equilibrium. Special cases are often easier, and a general result must agree with them.

meanings.short: Based on guesswork rather than firm evidence.
To write out or explain in full detail.
Something used in place of another thing, for the time being or for simplicity.
Strict and demanding; a stringent limit or test is hard to pass.
Large in amount or importance.
Hard to notice or understand, though it matters; needing care.
Hinting strongly at something without proving it.
A brief summary of the main points.
Following a fixed method; of an error, one that pushes every result the same way, so averaging does not remove it.
meanings.long: A systematic error comes from a flaw in the method, such as a badly set instrument; random errors average away, systematic ones do not.

meanings.short: Uncertainties that come from the method or the instruments and shift every result in the same direction.
meanings.long: Astronomers speak of "the systematics" of a survey, meaning the ways the method might bias all its results.

meanings.short: The main point to remember.

origin: Greek tauto, the same, and logos, saying.

meanings.short: A statement that is true just because of how it is worded, so it says nothing new.
Long, dull and repetitive, though not difficult.
Not certain or final; offered with caution.
The set of special words used in a subject.
Able to be checked by an experiment or observation.

everyday: In everyday English a theory is a hunch; in science it is a tested, coherent explanation.

meanings.short: An organised body of ideas, laws and methods about a subject: a tested explanation of nature, or a branch or method of mathematics.
meanings.long: General relativity is a theory in the sense of a tested explanation. In names like perturbation theory or number theory, the word means a systematic method or a field of study.

origin: Greek, a putting down or proposition.

meanings.short: A long research report written for a university degree, especially a doctorate.
meanings.long: A doctoral thesis presents a student's own new research; some important results first appeared in one.

meanings.short: An experiment carried out only in the imagination, to test what a theory predicts or to expose a contradiction.
meanings.long: A thought experiment follows a theory's rules through an imagined situation, such as a clock on a fast train or a box falling freely, where real measurement would be hard or impossible. Einstein used them to arrive at both theories of relativity.

meanings.short: So; as a result, or in this way.
meanings.long: "Thus" either draws a conclusion ("thus the energy is conserved") or points to a method ("written thus, the sum is easy").

meanings.short: Keeping terms only up to a stated power of a small quantity: to first order keeps the first power and drops squares and higher powers.
meanings.long: If ε is small, (1 + ε) squared is 1 + 2ε to first order, since ε squared is far smaller still. To second order means keeping the squares too, and dropping only cubes and higher powers.

meanings.short: With an error no larger than the stated amount.
meanings.long: "Accurate to within 1%" means the true value lies within 1% of the quoted one.

meanings.short: A set of methods that can be used together to solve a family of problems.
A deliberately oversimplified model, too crude to be realistic, used to show one idea clearly.
A balance between two things, where gaining more of one means losing some of the other.
A written record of exactly what was said in a recorded lecture, word for word.
meanings.long: MIT publishes a transcript of each video lecture. This site cites it by page ("transcript p. 3") to show where an idea or a spoken equation comes from.

meanings.short: A long, formal written work covering a subject in full.

everyday: Not "unimportant": in science it means "obvious" or "the simplest possible case".

meanings.short: So simple or obvious that it needs no argument; in maths, also the obvious zero solution.
meanings.long: "This step is trivial" means it follows at once. The trivial solution of an equation is the do-nothing one, such as everything equal to zero, which usually is not the one wanted.

meanings.short: A small typing mistake in a printed or written text.
Having only one possible meaning; perfectly clear.
To support from below; to be the basis of.
Impossible for a real physical system, such as a negative mass, a negative probability or a speed faster than light.
meanings.long: A mathematical solution can be unphysical: it solves the equations but breaks a condition nature imposes, so it is thrown away.

meanings.short: Not yet shown to be true.
Impossible to defend or keep believing, given the evidence.
Apart from a constant (or a sign, factor or phase): the two agree once that one difference is allowed for.
meanings.long: "The potential is fixed up to a constant" means any two answers differ only by adding a constant. "Equal up to a sign" means equal or opposite.

meanings.short: True or correctly applicable under the stated conditions.
meanings.long: A formula is valid in a certain range, such as low speeds; outside that range it may fail. A valid argument is one whose conclusion follows from its premises.

everyday: Usually not "disappear from sight": in maths and physics it mostly means "become zero".

meanings.short: To become zero; sometimes, of a fixed point or solution, to stop existing.
meanings.long: "The derivative vanishes at the top" means it is zero there. "Vanishes identically" means it is zero everywhere, for every value of the variable.

meanings.short: A final judgement on a question, after the evidence has been weighed.
Against, or compared with: sets two things side by side; a graph of y versus x has x along the bottom.
meanings.long: In science writing "plot A versus B" means draw A on the vertical axis and B on the horizontal one. In other places it simply contrasts two options.

origin: Latin via, way: so "by way of".

meanings.short: By way of; through, or by means of.
meanings.long: "Derived via the chain rule" means derived by using the chain rule. "Light reaches us via a lens" means it passes through the lens on its way.

meanings.short: The other way round: the same is true with the two things swapped.
meanings.long: "A pushes B and vice versa" means A pushes B and B pushes A. The phrase saves repeating a statement with its two parts exchanged.

meanings.short: Shown to have been right after earlier doubt.
Free of awkward features such as jumps, infinities or wild wiggles.
meanings.long: Physicists often assume their functions are well-behaved, so that derivatives and integrals exist and the usual rules apply.

meanings.short: Given a single clear meaning or value, without ambiguity or contradiction.
meanings.long: A quantity is well-defined when every allowed way of computing it gives the same answer.

meanings.short: While on the other hand: sets a contrasting fact beside the one just stated.
meanings.long: "Matter thins out as the universe grows, whereas vacuum energy stays the same."

meanings.short: Choosing one convenient case, because every other case works the same way, so nothing is lost by the choice.
meanings.long: Writers say this, often shortened to WLOG, when they put an axis along a vector or the origin at a point: any other choice would give the same result by symmetry.

meanings.short: A method or tool that is used all the time because it reliably does the job.
To give or produce as a result.
meanings.long: "Integrating yields the area" means the integration gives the area as its answer.

meanings.short: In chemical evolution, the mass of new heavy elements made per mass of gas locked into long-lived stars.
